title: Stability slate: load orchestration and seed care
content:
Purpose and high-level goal:

This is a working note for a parallel, guardrailed approach to throughput experiments that prioritizes repeatability across machine groups and time-of-day. The narrower objective: reduce run-to-run measurement noise by addressing orchestration-level causes (client pacing, RNG seeding, cached state priming, thermal-induced throttling) rather than only tweaking server internals.

Why I wrote this: runs from last month show ~6–12% wall-to-wall throughput variance on the same image and model when executed 24 hours apart. Theory so far: small differences in arrival jitter, cache residency from prior runs, and background thermal scaling are the bulk. We need a checklist + minimal config set to tame these.

Top-level strategy (short):
- Treat load generation as part of the system under test (SUT). Orchestrate seed hygiene, pacing, and priming in a reproducible manifest.
- Prefer deterministic RNG seeds (where possible) plus controlled entropy injection phases for robustness checks.
- Separate priming (stateful cache population) into an explicit phase with capture artifacts, then run measured windows that intentionally avoid boundary interactions (warmup -> hold -> drain).
- Instrument thermal and GPU clock telemetry and correlate with throughput windows. If thermal drift > threshold, mark run as contaminated.

Key definitions used in doc:
- priming: explicit population of model KV caches, shared runtime caches, and async floss (persistent small background services).
- anchor window: the measurement window used to report throughput (e.g., 10 minutes steady hold).
- seed manifest: ordered RNG seeds + request templates used by the load generator to ensure stimulus determinism.

Checklist: pre-run commands and validations
1) Node readiness
   - confirm GPU clocks pinned to expected profile (nvidia-smi -q | grep Clock)
   - check no long-running cron jobs or backups on nodes (ps aux | grep backup)
   - disable node autoscaling during experiment window (api call to infra)
2) Environment snapshot
   - capture image tag, kernel version, driver build, runtime binary sha (sha256sum)
   - upload snapshot to artifacts bucket before run start
3) Loadgen seed manifest
   - generate and freeze seed-manifest.json (list of seeds, templates, timestamps)
   - ensure every client instance receives the seed manifest at start-up
4) Controlled priming
   - run explicit priming phase: PRIMING_LEN = 5m with scripted request sequence -> capture KV cache hit rates
   - after priming, wait STABILIZE_PAUSE = 30s before entering anchor window
5) Anchor window sizing and guardrails
   - anchor window should be long enough to average microburst noise (recommended 5–15 minutes depending on concurrency)
   - collect per-token latency histograms, GPU util, and queue depths at 1s resolution
   - abort run if packet loss, ephemeral infra errors > 0.1%

Load generator config example (pseudo-yaml as text):

# loadgen config snippet (for reproducibility, cut/paste into job payload)
clients: 12
requests_per_client: infinity
arrival_pattern: deterministic-burst
seed_manifest_file: seeds/seed-manifest-2025-02-12.json
priming_phase:
  enabled: true
  sequence_file: priming-sequence.json
  duration_secs: 300
stabilize_pause_secs: 30
anchor_window_secs: 600
jitter_inject: {phase: robustness, percent: 0.5}  # optional
capture_metrics: [latency_histogram_1s, gpu_util_1s, p95_queue_depth_1s]

Seeding best practices (notes to self):
- Avoid using clock-based seeds (e.g., time() % N) for the main measurement runs. Use a deterministic master seed per experiment and derive per-client seeds via HMAC(master, client-id).
- Keep a copy of the seed-manifest with run artifacts so future debugging can replay exact request order.
- For stochastic robustness tests, run a set of N runs where we perturb the master seed and verify throughput remains within tolerance. Record both the seed and resulting metrics.

Priming heuristics and why they matter:
- Many throughput regressions are correlated with cold KV cache misses. By centralizing priming into a short, repeatable phase we reduce variance from implicit background traffic.
- Priming should attempt to mimic real request mix for cache residency; a degenerate priming set (all short prompts) biases the runtime toward short-path optimizations.
- Counter-intuitively, over-priming can saturate internal allocator state and change thermal profile. Keep priming bounded (5–10m) and validate with cache-hit telemetry.

Thermal and clocking considerations:
- Capture GPU and CPU clock frequencies at 1s granularity during priming -> anchor -> drain. If clock frequency drops >5% inside anchor window, mark run for exclusion.
- Where available, try to pin governors or use performance profiles to reduce DVFS noise. Document any infra-level overrides in the run artifact.

Repeatability scoring (quick heuristic):
- Create a run score combining: seed-determinism (30%), priming conformity (30%), clock stability (20%), infra noise flags (20%).
- A run with score < 0.8 is considered non-repeatable and should be discarded. Keep the scoring function simple and logged with artifacts.

Failure modes observed (real notes):
- run-2025-01-28: 11% lower throughput vs control; root cause: slow kernel upgrade on 2 nodes causing sporadic page reclaim spikes (was not visible in standard metrics).
- run-2025-01-31: 7% higher throughput; root cause: incidental warm caches from prior internal debug job (no priming phase used).
- run-2025-02-09: high p99 jitter; root cause: loadgen clients' NTP step on one client — clocks drifted by 300ms and arrival timestamps bunched up.

Analysis and correlation plan:
- Store per-run artifacts under artifacts/<date>/<run-id> including seed-manifest, priming-sequence, node snapshots, and telemetry exports.
- Always produce a small run-summary.csv with the scoring fields and verdict (accept/reject) to speed post-mortems.
- Automate a comparison job that overlays GPU clock traces with throughput to quickly highlight correlated drops.

Open questions / decisions to make:
- Should we always pin clocks for benchmark runs, or keep a separate set of experiments that expose DVFS behavior? (suggest: do both; primary baseline with pinned clocks)
- What's the minimum anchor window we can accept for 95% CI on throughput given current concurrency? Need to run a scaling experiment to compute minimal stable window per model size.
- How to handle multi-model fan-out runs where priming one model evicts caches of another? Option: isolated single-model runs + controlled fan-out experiments.

Action items (short):
- [ ] Codify seed-manifest format and add to loadgen repo (Priya)
- [ ] Add GPU/clock telemetry collector to the run scaffold (Jon)
- [ ] Run a 10x repeatability sweep with the exact guardrails for the 7B and 70B families (Luca)
- [ ] Draft a short Confluence page with the scoring rubric and artifact locations (Elena)

Notes to self (finish later):
- Consider adding a TTL to node provisioning so benchmark infra doesn't get reused by autopilot pools without reinitialization.
- Check if Prometheus scrape intervals are aligned with 1s telemetry collection (scrape_interval causes aliasing).

Appendix: quick example seed-manifest line (text):
{"seed": 123456789, "client_id": "c-03", "template": "summarize-news-128"}

End of draft. Will iterate after the first 10-run sweep and collect artifacts.
